block1.tip: Anak kalimat sifat menerangkan kata benda sebelumnya. Pilih kata penghubung dari kata benda itu: who untuk orang, which untuk benda, whose untuk kepemilikan, dan that bisa untuk orang atau benda.

lesson.intro: Anak kalimat sifat menerangkan kata benda sebelumnya, yang disebut antecedent. Dengan memilih kata penghubung yang tepat, kalimat menjadi lebih rinci dan tetap mudah dipahami.

sections.heading: Who, which, dan that
sections.bodyMd: **Who** untuk orang: **The teacher who helped me was kind.** **Which** untuk benda: **The book which I borrowed is about space.** **That** bisa untuk orang atau benda dalam anak kalimat yang perlu: **The bag that I bought is new.**

sections.heading: Whose dan whom
sections.bodyMd: **Whose** menunjukkan kepemilikan: **The student whose essay won is my friend.** **Whom** dipakai untuk orang sebagai objek: **The friend whom I met is nearby.** Dalam percakapan santai, whom sering diganti dengan who.

sections.heading: Anak kalimat yang perlu dan yang bisa dihilangkan
sections.bodyMd: Anak kalimat yang perlu tidak boleh dihilangkan, karena menentukan kata benda yang dimaksud. Anak kalimat yang bisa dihilangkan diapit koma dan hanya memberi tambahan: **The museum, which opened in 1950, has many maps.**

block3.title: Mencari Antecedent
block3.text:
Relative clauses help writers describe people, places, and things in more detail. A relative clause begins with a word such as who, whom, whose, which, or that. The word that a relative clause refers to is called the antecedent. For example, in the sentence The teacher who helped me was very kind, the antecedent is the teacher.

Many writers use relative clauses to define a term or specify a detail. Consider the sentence The museum, which opened in 1950, has a large collection of maps. Here the clause which opened in 1950 gives extra information about the museum. It does not change the main idea, so it can be removed without confusing the reader.

Some relative clauses are necessary. In the sentence The book that I borrowed is about space, the clause that I borrowed tells us which book the writer means. Without it, the sentence would not be clear. Good writers mention only the details that are needed to explain their meaning.

Writers also use whose to show possession. The student whose essay won the prize spoke first at the ceremony. The phrase whose essay won the prize can indicate that the essay belongs to the student. Whom is used for people as objects, as in The friend whom I met yesterday lives nearby.

Careful readers look for the antecedent before they choose the verb. Each relative clause must refer clearly to a noun, or the sentence can confuse the reader. A good editor will reveal such mistakes, and a good writer will check them before publishing. When you read a long text, try to identify the antecedent of each relative clause, and then explain to yourself why the clause is there.
